title: Raising the sparks
hookLine: holy sparks hide in everything, and ordinary acts done with care can lift them

lines: WASH A CUP. FOLD A SHIRT.
cards: You wash a cup. You answer an email. You fold a shirt, buy bread, sweep a floor.
Most of your day isn't dramatic. It can feel like the real life, the important, spiritual part, is happening somewhere else, and all this is just maintenance.

Hasidism took a picture from the kabbalah that turns that upside down. Hidden inside the cup, the email, the shirt and the bread are sparks of holiness, waiting. And the way you handle them can set them free.

teach.b: Tikkun means repair, mending, setting something right. The picture behind it comes from Rabbi Isaac Luria, a kabbalist in the town of Safed, whose teachings were written down mostly by his student, Chaim Vital.
When God made the world, Luria taught, divine light was poured into vessels that couldn't hold it. The vessels shattered.

Sparks of holy light scattered everywhere and fell into the world, trapped in shells, hidden in all things. The work of history is tikkun: gathering those sparks and lifting them back. That sounds cosmic, and it is.
But the Baal Shem Tov and the Hasidim brought it down to the kitchen.

teach.h: SPARKS IN FOOD, WORK AND WORDS.
teach.b: Sparks wait everywhere, they taught: in food, in work, in conversation, even in the people and places you happen to cross.
When you eat with a blessing, work honestly, speak kindly, do an ordinary thing with care, you lift the spark inside it.
A related phrase is tikkun olam, repairing the world, and it has old roots.
The Mishnah uses it for rules made for the good order of society, and the Aleinu prayer speaks of perfecting the world under the kingdom of the Almighty.
In modern times it has become a common name for justice and social action. The Hasidic version is quieter. The repair begins with how you wash this cup, right now.

how: Hasidim speak of raising sparks through blessings, prayer and everyday acts done with intention, and in modern usage tikkun olam names acts of justice and repair in the world.

o: repair, gathering scattered sparks of holy light
a vessel made to hold the divine light at creation
a blessing said before eating or drinking anything

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: brought the sparks into the kitchen

s: tikkun olam is a phrase invented in modern times
the Mishnah uses it, and the Aleinu prayer speaks of perfecting the world.
Luria's teachings were written down mostly by his student Chaim Vital
Vital is the main source for his teaching.
in Hasidic teaching, only prayer can lift a spark
eating, working and speaking with care can lift sparks too.

games.q: you're washing dishes and it feels pointless. what would a Hasid say is happening?
o: a spark may be waiting in this very task.
hurry up so you can pray.
games.why: Hasidism taught that sparks hide in ordinary things, and doing them with care lifts them.

practice: Choose one small task in front of you, a dish, a bed, a desk, and picture doing it slowly and fully: the water, the fabric, the weight of things. Imagine a spark inside it, waiting for someone to do this well.
If you pray, say a word of blessing before you begin.

wordCard.voice: Tikkun. Repair. In Luria's picture, holy sparks are scattered through everything, and ordinary acts done with care lift them back.

orig.note: Hebrew: repair, mending. Tikkun olam: repairing the world.

carryVoice: Your line: lift the sparks. The shattered light is waiting in plain things. Day three hundred ten, done.

sources.ref: Lurianic teaching on the breaking of the vessels and the raising of sparks (as recorded by Chaim Vital)
